title: Desiccation of the Aral Sea
summary: Soviet plans from 1959 made Central Asia a cotton supplier and diverted the Amu Darya and Syr Darya, starving the Aral Sea. NASA, citing geographer Philip Micklin, reports a loss of 88 percent of its surface area and 92 percent of its volume since 1960; USGS puts it at about a tenth of its 1960 size.

uncertainty.note: Process begins with river diversion from 1959-1960 and continues; the end year is the date of the NASA figures (2010), not an end of the process.

as_recorded.value: Since 1960, the Aral Sea has lost 88 percent of its surface area and 92 percent of its water volume
It is now only about 10% of the size it was in 1960
in 1959 when the Soviet Union picked Central Asia to serve as its cotton supplier

where.modern_name: Aral Sea (former sea), Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan (centre point)
where.historical_name: Aral Sea, Soviet Union (Kazakh and Uzbek SSRs)

importance.justification: One of the largest human-made environmental disasters of the 20th century, destroying a major inland sea.

reviewer_note: Figures differ by year and source: USGS says the sea once covered about 68,000 sq km and is now about 10% of its 1960 size; NASA/Micklin gives 88% area and 92% volume lost (2010); UN Chronicle says only that it shrank to half its size (1999 text). The UNEP foresight brief (area halved and volume down 75% by the late 1980s, over 90% total) could not be fetched, so is not cited. No animation added: NASA attributes its figures to one expert.
